newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban accuse India of supporting opposition.
newsitem.headline: Taleban accuse India of supporting opposition.

text.p: An official of the Taleban administration in Afghanistan said on Saturday India was supporting the anti-Taleban alliance and suggested Delhi was trying to sour the country's relations with Pakistan,

"For the last 18 years the Indian government has stood against our national interest. India is still supporting the Rabbani regime and is still giving them assistance." acting deputy foreign minister Sher Abbas Stanakzai told Reuters in an interview.

The Taleban have frequently accused India, along with Russia and Iran, of supporting the forces of President Burhanuddin Rabbani, who was driven from Kabul in September last year when the Taleban took the city.
Both India and Rabbani, now a leading member of the anti-Taleban alliance, have denied the accusations.
However, Stanakzai did hold out a chance of normalisation of relations between the Taleban and India.

"If India stops its interference in Afghanistan and they are willing to have good relations with us, it is in our interest. We would be willing to rethink our policies and there is the possibility that we cnn have normal relations with India." he said.
Stanakzai said rumours that Pakistan, India's traditional enemy, was supporting certain anti-Taleban elements were being spread by people hoping to damage relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan.
"I think that some of our enemies are very keen to use the situation to harm relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan." he said.
He said that there was no proof that there had been official Pakistani support for a recent uprising in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar.
"There is no proof that the Pakistani government helped the opposition in Kunar, and we would not expect tham to help." Stanakzai said.
In a recently published interview Stanakzai said Pakistan
would be wary of supporting any opposition force in Afghanistan because it would drive the government into the arms of the Indians.
He said it was natural that some of the thousands of Afghan refugees still residing in Pakistan would be opposed to the administation he represented.
"It is normal that some of our opposition should be living in the (refugee) camps in Pakistan. Many people escaped to Pakistan when we took over the provinces and they are armed." he said.

The Taleban now control almost 80 per cent of Afghanistan but face opposition forces on front lines in the foothills of the Hindu Kush mountains, some 120 kilometers (75 miles) north of Kabul and in the remote nortwestern provinces of the country.
